newsitem.title: YEMEN: Polish hostages in Yemen released - official.
newsitem.headline: Polish hostages in Yemen released - official.

text.p: Five Polish tourists held hostage by Yemeni tribesmen since last week were released by their abductors on Wednesday, an official Yemeni source said.
"The hostages were released a few hours ago...They are on their way to Sanaa accompanied by security forces," the official told Reuters.
The official declined to comment on reports earlier on Wednesday that Yemen had assured the kidnappers they would not be prosecuted for the kidnapping or for attacking security forces.
On Friday, the tribesmen fired rocket-propelled grenades at military forces who had surrounded them, killing three soldiers and wounding five.
Stanislaw Smolen, Polish consul to Sanaa, told Reuters on Wednesday that Yemen had assured the abductors that they would not be prosecuted for the kidnapping or for the attack on security forces.
"The kidnappers received today a letter of guarantee from the government that they will not be punished after the release of the hostages,"

The tourists -- three men and two women between the ages of 50 and 64 -- were kidnapped on their way to archaeological sites in western Yemen last week. It was the second abduction of European holidaymakers within a month.
The tourists were abducted by members of the Al al-Masni tribe in the Khawlan area, about 65-km (40-miles) east of the capital Sanaa.
Polish officials have declined to name the hostages.

A leading member of a club devoted to foreign travel told Gazeta Wyborcza newspaper she believed they were from the Polish Explorers's Society and had left on December 10 for a tour of Yemen, Ethiopia and Sudan. She said they included a freelance journalist and a couple of physicists.
Yemeni authorities on December 19 freed five Dutch tourists who were abducted and briefly held by tribesmen while touring an area 240-km (150-miles) north of Sanaa.

In recent years, tribes in Yemen with grievances against the government or foreign oil firms have kidnapped tourists or other foreigners to use as bargaining chips. The tribes' demands have usually involved land or water issues, and have rarely been political.
